claims.claim: Social development is the growth of a child's social skills, emotions, and relationships with other people across childhood; in the lifespan-development account it is tracked as a widening social world from caregivers to peers and the skills that come with each step.

Children learn to recognize and manage their feelings gradually, and emotion regulation is a developmental achievement of early childhood (identifying emotions, calming, waiting, recovering from upsets).
Peers are children similar in age or in cognitive, physical, and emotional development; after parents and siblings they are the largest socializing agent in young childhood.

Play spans solitary, parallel, associative, and cooperative forms (after Mildred Parten's framework), and social play such as associative and cooperative play helps children develop communication skills, emotion regulation, and conflict-resolution skills and is essential to forming and maintaining friendships; unstructured child-led play teaches turn-taking, sharing, and cooperation.

CDC developmental milestones describe what most children do by given ages: most 2-year-olds notice when others are hurt or upset and look at a caregiver's face to see how to react; most 3-year-olds notice other children and join them to play and can calm down within minutes after a caregiver leaves; many 4-year-olds pretend to be something else during play, ask to play with other children, and comfort others who are hurt or sad.

Self-concept is the abstract, cognitive idea of who you are — all the beliefs you have about yourself; at about age three it holds basic facts (name, age, gender, relations), and by the school years it grows to include abilities and personality traits.

Self-esteem is a personal evaluation of the self — whether you hold yourself in high regard or feel critical about yourself; in early childhood most children base their self-esteem on feedback from parents and caregivers, and children who experience love, support, and encouragement tend to develop relatively high self-esteem.

Erik Erikson's psychosocial theory (published 1950; expanded 1963) describes eight stages of development, each a conflict between the person and the social world: trust versus mistrust, autonomy versus shame and doubt, initiative versus guilt, industry versus inferiority, identity versus role confusion, intimacy versus isolation, generativity versus stagnation, and integrity versus despair.

Erikson's psychosocial theory frames development as continuing across the whole lifespan, with social relationships shaping the sense of self at every stage; each stage involves a central conflict whose resolution builds a psychological strength.

Temperament consists of the innate biological components of individuality present from birth; its traits are fairly consistent and stable over time. Thomas and Chess identified three temperament clusters — easy, difficult, and slow to warm up — and goodness of fit, the match between the child's temperament and the environment, matters for how well the child fares.

positions: Thomas and Chess described temperament clusters (easy, difficult, slow to warm up) as stable early styles.
Later models (e.g., Rothbart) treat temperament traits as developing and modifiable, and the goodness-of-fit idea shows environment matters.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states temperament is biologically based and fairly stable but shapes rather than decides development, citing goodness of fit — no temperament label is treated as a verdict.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Ages attached to Erikson's stages vary across sources.
positions: OpenStax Lifespan Development Table 1.1 gives stage ages of 0-1, 1-3, 3-6, 7-11, 12-18, 19-29, 30-64, and 65+.
Simply Psychology gives somewhat different ranges (e.g., 0-18 months, 18 months-3 years, 3-5 years).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names all eight stages with one line each and gives no ages, avoiding the discrepancy entirely; the framework is attributed to Erikson (1950, 1963).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Milestone ages vary from child to child.
positions: CDC lists milestones as things most children do by a given age.
Individual children develop socially at different rates, and culture shapes expectations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses typical-range framing ('most children,' 'many four-year-olds') attributed to the CDC, with no deadline or alarm language and no pathologizing.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate framing that social development is merely 'a foundational concept' used to 'organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships' — discarded as machine-generated filler with no domain content.
The draft's generic objectives and vocabulary ('context,' 'evidence,' 'application') that named no actual concepts of social development — replaced with sourced domain content.
The draft's 'worked example' describing a generic student reading a scenario — replaced with an original, discipline-specific playground example.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire machine-generated draft (definition, objectives, vocabulary, mistakes, example) with source-verified content.
Kept Erikson's stage names in the wording used by OpenStax Lifespan Development (e.g., 'identity versus role confusion') and omitted stage ages to avoid cross-source discrepancies.
Framed CDC milestones as typical ranges with 'most children' language per the subject's cautions; no absolute deadlines.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 1.3: Major Theories and Theorists
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. openstax.org blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture 20251118230710 of the canonical URL. Supports: Erikson's psychosocial theory of development (Erikson, 1950, 1963) and Table 1.1 listing all eight stages — trust versus mistrust (0-1), autonomy versus shame/doubt (1-3), initiative versus guilt (3-6), industry versus inferiority (7-11), identity versus confusion (12-18), intimacy versus isolation (19-29), generativity versus stagnation (30-64), integrity versus despair (65+) — each with a one-line developmental task. Also supports the framing that each stage is a psychosocial mastery opportunity building on the previous one. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 4.2: Temperament and Personality in Infants and Toddlers
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture (2025) of the canonical URL. Supports: temperament as the innate biological components of individuality present from birth, with traits fairly consistent and stable over time; Thomas and Chess's (1977) nine-trait model and three clusters — easy, difficult, slow to warm up — with roughly 65% of infants fitting one of the three; goodness of fit as the match between temperament and environment (Thomas & Chess); Rothbart's surgency/negative affectivity/effortful control as a later model. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 6.1: Social and Emotional Development in Early Childhood
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture (2025) of the canonical URL. Supports: emotion regulation as a developmental achievement of early childhood and the role of recognizing and validating children's emotions; self-concept defined as an abstract, cognitive idea of who you are including all beliefs about yourself, simple at age three (name, gender, age, relations) and richer by age eight (hobbies, traits); self-esteem defined as a personal evaluation of the self, in early childhood based largely on feedback from parents and caregivers; Erikson's third stage (initiative versus guilt, 1950) and the stage sequence it builds on; the widening social domain of early childhood (peers, extended family, preschool). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Erik Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live 2026-08-22. Corroborates: Erikson (1902-1994) proposed a lifespan model in which social relationships shape the sense of self, with eight stages each marked by a central psychosocial conflict (trust vs. mistrust through ego integrity vs. despair), and successfully resolving each conflict builds a psychological strength. Used only for the one-line attribution and stage naming; its differing age ranges were deliberately not used (see conflictingEvidence).
